newsitem.title: USA: Computer beats Kasparov to tie match 1-1.
newsitem.headline: Computer beats Kasparov to tie match 1-1.

text.p: The supercomputer Deep Blue, playing in a style usually seen in human players, defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov on Sunday to tie their six-game $1.1 million re-match at one win each.
Deep Blue's victory after 45 moves and 3 hours and 42 minutes play was only the second time in history that a computer programme had beaten a reigning world champion in a classical chess format.
The first time was in February 1996 in Philadelphia when the system won the opening game against Kasparov in the first match of a intense rivalry pitting human brain against silicon chip.

"This was real chess, not computer chess," Deep Blue's grandmaster consultant Joel Benjamin of the United States told hundreds of spectators who watched the second game of the contest in a Manhattan office complex.

Benjamin and other expert observers said the computer established a spacial advantage out of the opening, restricting the 34-year-old Russian grandmaster to mostly passive moves. Usually, computers excel at complicated tactical struggles in which their massive calculating powers give them the edge, but in this game, a modified and enhanced Deep Blue demonstrated that it "understood" positional concepts too, the experts said.

The match was tied at one point each. One point is awarded for a victory and a half-point for a draw. Kasparov won the first game with the white pieces on Saturday. The winner will receive $700,000 and the loser $400,000. The third game was scheduled for Tuesday and the match ends on May 11.

"It was easily the best game I've ever seen a computer play and one of the best games I've ever seen anything play against Kasparov," said Frederic Friedel, the creator of chess-playing computer called "Fritz" and one of the Russian's closest advisors. "It played very intelligent chess and this is what we've always been slightly afraid of."

Grandmasters watched in awe as Deep Blue and Kasparov opened the game with the classical Ruy Lopez or Spanish game, sometimes referred to as "the Spanish torture". The system is named after a chess-playing Spanish priest who lived in the 16th century.

The clash between Kasparov and the machine is part chess match and part research project to help build computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations at high speeds. Among the applications for the technology developed for Deep Blue are weather forecasting, air traffic control, data mining and molecular dynamics.

Chess playing is considered ideal for computers because the game involves a specific number of physical objects governed by simple, clearly defined rules. Information on the contest is carried on the IBM Web site www.chess.ibm.com.
IBM officials said that in Saturday's first game, the site received more than 5 million retrievals from all over the world during the opening hour alone.

Kasparov, considered by most experts to be the best player in the history of chess, has no advance information of Deep Blue's most recent games or improvements made to its programme. Deep Blue, an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess, calculates hundreds of millions of moves per second.
IBM computer scientists have also infused Deep Blue with more knowledge of chess with the help of Benjamin, a former U.S. champion.

"We really didn't make many adjustments last night, some tuning, but no basic changes it's still early in the match," team manager Chung-Jen Tan told reporters. "It's made out of a different species than real grandmasters."
Some grandmasters were beginning to believe otherwise after Sunday's performance.

"I think the computer played an excellent positional game and I was impressed by how it closed all the possible counterplay Kasparov may have dreamed of," said Czech-born grandmaster Lubo Kavalek, who now lives in the Washington D.C. area. "It was incredibly well done."
